Design: Engineering students were presented real world
problems and obstacles faced by people lacking upper limb
function. Working as teams, students proposed novel engi-
neering solutions. Fully working prototypes were constructed,
tested, and re ﬁned until a ﬁnal design was reached meeting the
expectations of the user/project sponsor. Formal presentations
and written reports were prepared for the user/project sponsor.
Final designs were displayed at the College of Engineering
Design Showcase.
Setting: State-of-the-art machine shop with computer-aided
(Solid Works) equipment and fabrication (3D Printing). Assembly
and testing for safety, reliability, and durability performed before
ﬁeld testing with the user/sponsor.
Participants: Twenty seven students participated (10 women, 17
men) with 10 majoring in Mechanical Engineering (ME), 11
majoring in Bioengineering (BioE), and 6 dual majoring in ME/
BioE.
Interventions: Qualitative/quantitative questionnaire given to
each student assessed satisfaction with the prototype device, intra-
team relationships, and communications with the user/sponsor.
Similar questionnaire was given to the user assessing satisfaction
with the prototype device, likelihood of continued use, and team
communication.
Main Outcome Measures: Student/user satisfaction with the
devices was uniformly high. Successful communication, teamwork,
and leadership strongly correlated with degree of interaction
between team and user.
Results or Clinical Course: Team #1: collapsible shooting
stick to support ri ﬂe barrel for one -armed hunter. Team #2: self-
standing tote bag for user with no grasp or pinch ability. Team
#3: device to swipe credit card at ATM or gas pump without
pinch ability. Team #4: device to zip up a jacket single handed.
Teams #5/6: device to hold feeding utensils for user without use
of ﬁngers.
Conclusions: Senior engineering students can produce workable
prototype devices of suf ﬁciently high quality while gaining
perspectives on the needs of disabled persons. This study generated
practical lessons for engineering students preparing to enter
industry.
Poster 90
Intrathecal Baclofen Pump Placement in a Patient
with Stiff Person Syndrome: A Case Report.
Ron Avraham, MD (Temple University Hospital,
Philadelphia, PA, United States); Annu Sharma, DO;
Ryan Channick, MD; Carmen A. Angles, MD.
Disclosures: R. Avraham, No Disclosures: I Have No Relevant
Financial Relationships to Disclose.
Case Description: A 32-year-old woman, recently diagnosed
with stiff person syndrome and postural orthostatic tachycardia
syndrome (POTS), presented with progressive upper and lower
limb weakness and spasticity within a 5-year period. Physical
examination ﬁndings were signiﬁcant for increased tone in the
upper and lower limbs and dystonia, suggestive of a mixed
movement disorder with spontaneously occurring painful muscle
spasms.
Setting: Inpatient Rehabilitation Unit at an Academic Medical
Center.
Results or Clinical Course: During her rehabilitation stay, the
patient underwent diagnostic workup that included testing for
anti- glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibody, which was
negative, thus making the case for stiff person syndrome based on
clinical examination. She received carbamazepine 200 mg twice
per day, which managed her painful contractions, and oral
baclofen for spasticity control. An intrathecal baclofen pump

placed later in her rehabilitation stay signi ﬁcantly improved her
spasticity and her ability to achieve functional goals in
rehabilitation.
Discussion: Stiff person syndrome is a rare neurological
disorder characterized by rigidity in the symmetrical paraspinal
and abdominal muscles, increased lordosis, a “tin soldier ” gait
pattern, and episodic spasms, which occur in response to
environmental stimuli. Diagnostic testing includes electro-
diagnostic studies and laboratory testing for glutamic acid
decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies, which is seronegative in 40% of
the population. Baclofen (a gamma-aminobutyric acid (a GABAb
agonist) acts to restore the balance of excitatory and inhibitory
input to reduce muscle hyperactivity and spasticity. Intrathecal
baclofen pumps deliver baclofen directly to the intrathecal space
and may be used to manage spasticity when oral therapy has
proven inadequate.
Conclusions: This case highlights the use of an intrathecal
baclofen pump for management of spasticity in a patient with
clinical ﬁndings of stiff person syndrome.
Poster 91
Serotonin Syndrome in Chronic Kidney Disease
Patient after Given a Dose of Duloxetine while on
Trazodone: A
Case Report.
Chau Uong, DO (Marianjoy Rehabilitation Hospital,
Wheaton, IL, United States); Padma Srigiriraju, MD.
Disclosures: C. Uong, No Disclosures: I Have No Relevant
Financial Relationships to Disclose.
Case Description: A 50-year-old woman with underlying
chronic kidney disease stage IV who suffered a cerebrovascular
accident status post coronary artery bypass graft underwent acute
inpatient rehabilitation. While there, she was started on trazodone
for insomnia. About 1
1/2 weeks later, metaxalone was started for
leg cramps but because it was not effective, metaxalone was
switched to Lioresal instead. The following day (which was about 2
weeks after starting trazodone), she received one dose of duloxetine
for symptoms of depression and became more lethargic and
nauseous. The next day, she became extremely agitated, confused,
withdrawn, tachycardic, and had dilated pupils, incoherent speech,
and abdominal pain.
Setting: Freestanding rehabilitation hospital and acute care
hospital,
Results or Clinical Course: The patient was sent to the ER,
where the initial thought was anticholinergic syndrome from
Lioresal. Head CT and MRI of the brain were negative for acute
changes. She was admitted to the ICU for protection of the airway.
